items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: All the tenor players nowadays sound like John Coltrane.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: They’re all Coltrane disciples. All of them are Charlie Parker’s disciples.

ctx.x: So, you weren’t going to change with any fad.

No, whatever anybody’s doing that’s their thing, I’m not going to try….the old saying in New York used to be, they would rather be the world’s worst originator than to be the world’s greatest imitator. Which I agree with. Because if you’re an originator, I don’t care how bad it is, it’s your sound. And if you stick with it, somebody’s going to like it. And if you’re an imitator, you’ll never surpass the one that originated that style that you’re copying, that you’re emulating. You can never capture nobody else’s…

influence on the alto players. If you hear one tenor player, you hear them all. They’re all Coltrane disciples. All of them are Charlie Parker’s disciples. There was a few things that Charlie Parker played the melody wrong, so everybody started playing the melody wrong because he did it. And, Dizzy, I remember when Dizzy used to play just like Roy Eldridge, exactly just like Roy Eldridge. But he got to the point where he was going to think for himself, like Roy thought for himself, so he created him another style…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee mentions John Coltrane only in the context of the interviewer's statement about white prejudice and musical trends; the interviewee does not describe a personal interaction or professional relationship with Coltrane.

ctx.x: So why, why, why do that? Why? You should be able to answer that more --

It's a form of white prejudice. There's no question about it. The only thing is, where I find it very hypocritical, here he comes along, now, if I said to one of these people now, I've been playing Ben Webster, Don Byas, Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins records, and I never play Coltrane's records because I can't stand them. Now they will say that I'm living in the past. But the same people, when this kid comes along, and he deserves a lot of credit because he's reviving something that deserves reviving, but the…
See, they don't listen. They can't be bothered to listen to Ben Webster on the old records, and so on.
